result.summary: Juno sends Iris to rouse Turnus, who attacks the Trojan camp while Æneas is away and tries to burn the fleet, but the ships become sea-nymphs. Nisus and Euryalus raid the Rutulian camp by night and are killed. Turnus then breaks into the camp, kills many, and is driven into the Tiber.

scenes.title: Iris rouses Turnus
scenes.summary: Iris tells Turnus that Æneas is away at Evander's city. Turnus prays and leads his army to the Trojan camp.
scenes.stakes: Turnus risks losing the chance to strike the Trojans while Æneas is absent.

scenes.title: Siege of the Trojan camp
scenes.summary: The Trojans obey Æneas's order to stay behind their walls. Turnus circles the camp like a wolf and fires the fleet.
scenes.stakes: The Trojan ships and camp are threatened with burning.

scenes.title: The ships become sea-nymphs
scenes.summary: The poet tells how Cybele once begged Jove to make her pine ships immortal. Now her voice frees them and they turn into sea-goddesses.
scenes.stakes: The fleet faces destruction by fire.

scenes.title: Turnus's defiance and the watch
scenes.summary: Turnus dismisses the portent and vows to besiege the camp. Both sides set their watches for the night.
scenes.stakes: Turnus stakes his claim to Lavinia; the Trojans risk being trapped.

scenes.title: Nisus and Euryalus volunteer
scenes.summary: Nisus proposes slipping through the lines to fetch Æneas, and Euryalus insists on joining him. The council accepts, Iulus promises rewards, and Euryalus entrusts his mother to Iulus's care.
scenes.stakes: The two friends risk death, and the camp needs Æneas's return.

scenes.title: Slaughter in the Rutulian camp
scenes.summary: Nisus and Euryalus kill many sleeping Rutulians and take spoils, including Messapus's helmet.

scenes.title: Death of the two friends
scenes.summary: Volscens's horsemen spot the helmet and catch Euryalus in the wood. Nisus kills two men and then Volscens, and dies over his friend.
scenes.stakes: Their lives, and Euryalus in particular.

scenes.title: The mother's lament
scenes.summary: The heads of the two are paraded on spears. Euryalus's mother hears and wails at the walls until she is carried away.
scenes.stakes: A mother loses her only son.

scenes.title: Assault and Ascanius's first kill
scenes.summary: The Rutulians storm the walls and Turnus burns a tower. Ascanius kills the boastful Numanus.

scenes.title: Apollo restrains Ascanius
scenes.summary: Apollo praises Ascanius, then, disguised as Butes, tells him to stop fighting.
scenes.stakes: The young heir could be killed.

scenes.title: Turnus inside the camp
scenes.summary: Pandarus and Bitias open the gate. Turnus enters, kills many, but is overwhelmed and escapes by leaping into the Tiber.
scenes.stakes: Turnus's life, and the Trojans' camp.

alias_notes.explanation: Remulus is given as Numanus's surname.

notable_quotes.reason: The poet's tribute promising immortal fame to Nisus and Euryalus.
Apollo's praise of Ascanius, 'thus men climb the stars'.

analysis.text: Love between friends and the glory and cost of daring deeds are shown in the Nisus and Euryalus episode, where ambition and excess of slaughter cause their doom.
The poet looks to Rome's lasting power on the Capitol, tying epic fighting to Augustan ideals of Roman destiny.

legacy.text: The Nisus and Euryalus episode influenced later epics such as Tasso's Gerusalemme liberata, with its pair Clorinda-like night raids, and was widely imitated.

fun_facts.text: The transformation of the ships into nymphs echoes the Homeric account of the Phaeacian ship turned to stone.

language_notes.text: "Child of Thaumas" is Iris, the rainbow goddess and messenger, daughter of Thaumas in Greek myth.
"Bespoke" here means "addressed" or "spoke to", not "ordered in advance".
The Palatine is the hill where Evander's settlement stood, later the site of Rome.
Corythus is an Etruscan city; the "Lydian bands" are the Etruscans, traditionally said to have come from Lydia.
The sky seeming to part and the stars to reel is Turnus's reading of Iris's appearance as a divine sign.
"Presage" means omen or foretelling; "whoe'er" is "whoever".
Taking up river water is a ritual purification before prayer and battle.
"Richly dowered" means richly endowed or supplied; "broidered" means embroidered.
Teucrians: another name for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.
"Quick with the steel" is an elliptical command: be quick to take up your swords and weapons.
Helm: an archaic word for helmet. The scarlet crest was a plume on top of it.
"The overture of battle" means that the thrown javelin acts as the opening move, like a ritual first strike.
Rutulian: Turnus is king of the Rutulians, an Italian people.
"Fire-god" is Vulcan, used here for fire itself.
Teucrians is another name for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.
Berecyntian refers to Berecyntus, a Phrygian mountain sacred to Cybele; here it is a title for the great mother.
"Fain" means gladly or willing; "Dardany" is Troy's land, named for Dardanus, so "youth of Dardany" means Æneas.
"Have charter of immortality" means hold a legal right or guarantee of never dying.
Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy; Laurentian soil is the territory around Laurentum, where the Trojans are to settle.
Jove swears by the Styx, the underworld river of his brother Pluto; an oath by it was the gods' most binding.
"Quarter of the dawn-goddess" means the east, where Aurora, the dawn, rises.
"One half of nature" means the sea, one of two elements for travel; with the land held by Italians, the Trojans are cut off from both.
"Vaunt" means to boast of. Turnus mocks the Trojans' prophecies as empty bragging.
The Atridæ (Agamemnon and Menelaus) went to war over Helen's abduction by Paris. Turnus compares his stolen bride Lavinia to Helen.
Turnus says Troy's one destruction should suffice; had one offence over a woman been enough, the Trojans would now hate all women.
Neptune and Apollo were said to have built Troy's walls, yet the city still fell to the Greeks.
Vulcan made Achilles' armour for Thetis; Turnus says he needs no divine arms or Greek-sized fleet. The Etruscans were allied with Æneas.
Refers to the Greeks' theft of the Palladium (Troy's guardian image), the killing of sentries, and the wooden horse. Turnus scorns such stealth.
Danaans and Pelasgians are names for the Greeks.
"Leaguer" means to besiege or blockade.
"Give wine its fling" means to drink freely; "tilt the brazen bowl" means to drain bronze cups.
Ida the huntress: Nisus's mother was a nymph of Mount Ida, near Troy, who hunted there; hence his skill with javelin and arrow.
"Wont" means were accustomed; the bracketed number is a footnote marker from the edition, not Virgil's text.
Argive terrors and Trojan agonies: Argive means Greek; Euryalus refers to the Trojan War and the fall of Troy, which he lived through.
The rites of the absent: a cenotaph, an empty tomb, honoured a person whose body could not be recovered. Ancient belief held that unburied dead found no rest.
"Guerdons" is an archaic word for rewards.
Household gods are the Penates, protectors of the family. Vesta was goddess of the hearth, and her shrine was kept by the Trojans.
Sidonian Dido: Dido, queen of Carthage, came from Phoenician Sidon and gave Æneas gifts in Book 1. Arisba was a town near Troy.
Creusa was Æneas's wife and Iulus's mother, lost during the escape from Troy. Swearing by one's own head was a solemn oath.
"Deliver them cancelled to the clouds" means the winds carry the words away and make them void.
An augur was a priest who foretold events from omens such as bird flight; Rhamnes' skill failed to foresee his own death.
"Shears" means cuts through; "lops" means cuts off. Both are violent verbs for beheading.
"Played" refers to gaming, probably dice; the sentence wishes he had played until morning and survived.
"Forbear we now" is an archaic exhortation meaning "let us stop now."
"Fain" means gladly or eagerly; Cædicus wanted to win Remulus' friendship from afar by sending the gift.
"Sent on from the town of Latium": the cavalry come from the Latin city, carrying a message to Turnus, leader of the Rutulians.
"Gallants" is the translator's word for brave young men; Volscens is addressing the two strangers brusquely.
"Ilex" is the holm oak, a dark evergreen tree; "shagged" means rough and overgrown.
The region "afterwards called Alban" refers to Alba Longa, the city Ascanius would later found, so the poet looks ahead to a later age.
Latona's daughter is the moon goddess and huntress Diana (the Greek Artemis); Nisus, a hunter, appeals to her as patron.
"Both debts" means the deaths of Sulmo and Tagus, which Volscens will make Euryalus repay with his life.
The Capitol was Rome's sacred hill. The poet promises that the fame of the pair will last as long as Roman rule.
Tithonus was a Trojan prince loved by Aurora, goddess of dawn; her rising from his couch is a stock poetic way to say daybreak.
"The thread ran back": the spindle unwound as she dropped it, showing the sudden shock of the news.
"Ravin" means prey or plunder; here it is the devouring of her son's body by dogs and birds.
"Penthouse of shields" is the testudo, soldiers holding shields overhead and interlocked like a tortoise shell to ward off missiles.
Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry; the poet invokes her before the great battle narrative, as Homer did.
"Twice-captured Phrygians": Numanus taunts the Trojans (Phrygians) as defeated once at Troy and now again besieged. Phrygian was used contemptuously for Trojan.
The Atridæ are Agamemnon and Menelaus, Greek leaders at Troy; Ulysses was famed for cunning speech. Numanus says the Trojans face tougher foes now.
Dindymus is a mountain in Phrygia sacred to Cybele, the Great Mother, whose worship used pipes and cymbals; Numanus mocks Trojans as effeminate.
Thunder on the left was a favourable omen in Roman belief, signalling Jove's assent to Ascanius's prayer.
"Son of gods that are, sire of gods that shall be": Ascanius (Iulus) descends from Venus and will father the Alban line and ancestors of Rome's deified Caesars.
"Kid-stars" are the Haedi, a constellation whose setting brought stormy weather.
A phalaric lance (phalarica) was a heavy missile spear, hurled with great force.
Inarime lies on the giant Typhœus, who was imprisoned beneath it by Jove; the island's rumblings were said to be his struggles.
Turnus compares himself to Achilles, who brought death to Priam's Troy; he threatens Trojans as Greeks once did.
"Saturnian Juno" means Juno, daughter of Saturn.
Jove sends Iris to warn Juno, his sister and wife, to stop aiding Turnus, so she withdraws her support.

context_notes.text: Juno, queen of the gods, favours the Latins and opposes the Trojans, so she sends Iris to stir Turnus to attack.
Pilumnus is Turnus's ancestor, a Latin deity or hero, so the grove is a family sacred place.
Messapus is a Latin ally of Turnus; Tyrrheus was the herdsman whose sons were involved in starting the war.
Æneas has gone to seek allies upriver, leaving orders that the camp must not fight in the open while he is away.
The Trojan ships are drawn up beside the camp. Turnus's attack on them threatens the Trojans' only way home.
Cybele, the Phrygian mother of the gods, was worshipped on Mount Ida, where Æneas cut the timber for his ships.
Doto and Galatea are Nereids, sea-nymphs who were daughters of the sea-god Nereus.
Turnus, leader of the Rutulians, is attacking the Trojan camp and has tried to set the ships on fire.
The portent is the burning of the Trojan ships, which turned into sea-nymphs. Turnus tries to reinterpret it as a bad omen for the Trojans.
Mnestheus and Serestus are Trojan captains left in charge of the camp while Æneas is away seeking allies.
Nisus and Euryalus are Trojans left guarding the camp while Æneas is away seeking allies. Turnus and the Rutulians are besieging it.
Pallanteum is the city of the Arcadian king Evander, Æneas's ally, where he has gone for help.
Iulus is the young son of Æneas, also called Ascanius. He acts as leader in his father's absence.
Euryalus's mother is among the Trojan women who chose to follow the fleet rather than stay in Sicily with Acestes.
Nisus, son of Hyrtacus, and the young Euryalus are Trojans raiding the sleeping Rutulian camp by night to reach Æneas.
Messapus was a Rutulian ally; wearing his helmet will make Euryalus conspicuous, and the shining helm helps lead to the pair's discovery.
Euryalus wears the helmet taken as spoil from the slain Rutulian Messapus's men; its shine gives the pair away.
The Rutulians are Turnus's people, enemies of the Trojans. Nisus tries to draw their anger from Euryalus onto himself.
The Trojans hold the camp; the river Tiber guards its right side, so the enemy attacks mainly from the left.
Mezentius is the exiled Etruscan king allied with Turnus, known for contempt of the gods.
Ascanius, also called Iulus, is Æneas' young son, here in his first act of war.
Apollo supports the Trojans here; Ascanius has just killed Numanus with an arrow, his first feat in battle.
Anchises was Æneas' father; Butes was his old armour-bearer and gatekeeper, so Ascanius would trust his words.
Pandarus and Bitias guard the gate on Æneas' orders while he is away; they open it out of overconfidence.
Amata is Latinus' queen and Turnus' ardent supporter; Ardea is Turnus' home city.

literary_notes.text: "Now, now" and the string of commands convey urgency, pushing Turnus toward action.
Iris's departure, trailing her bow across the clouds, paints the rainbow as a visible sign of divine presence.
Comparing Turnus to the Ganges and the Nile suggests a vast, calm, powerful force that is about to flood forward.
The Trojans' shame and anger held in check by obedience show their discipline and loyalty to Æneas.
Turnus looks for an opening "where way is none," showing his strength is useless against the walls.
Turnus is compared to a hungry wolf outside a sheepfold, making the Trojans helpless lambs and showing his frustrated, predatory rage.
The Fire-god stands for fire, giving the burning a divine, menacing presence.
The poet addresses the Muses directly, asking for their help in telling a hard-to-believe tale, as epic poets traditionally do.
The strange light and cloud with a terrifying voice announce the divine intervention before it is explained.
The ships dive like dolphins, a vivid image that prepares for their change into sea creatures.
Tiber is shown pausing, murmuring and turning back, as if the river itself shared the awe of the armies.
Turnus's unshaken confidence and ready speech show him as bold and rash, dismissing omens.
"My Trojan war" casts Turnus as a new Greek hero and Æneas as a new Paris, framing the conflict as a replay of Troy.
Turnus scorns night raids as cowardly, yet Nisus and Euryalus will soon attack by night; his boast about daylight and fire is undercut.
Bright fires and revelling guards paint a vivid, relaxed Rutulian camp, contrasting with the tense Trojans and hinting at carelessness.
Nisus asks whether his urge is divine or merely personal, which raises the question of whether the coming venture is wise or reckless.
Euryalus's contempt for life shows his youthful, headlong courage and the readiness for glory that will drive the episode.
Aletes addresses the absent gods directly, turning the young men's courage into a sign of divine favour toward Troy.
Euryalus leaves without telling his mother. The reader senses how heavily this will weigh once the venture goes wrong.
The winds are shown scattering and handing over the prayers as if they were agents, suggesting the futility of these hopes.
The closing phrase warns that the pair will kill many before their own deaths, and prepares for the night raid and its tragedy.
Serranus' wish that his play had lasted until morning gives pathos: the pleasure that kept him awake left him defenceless.
Nisus' killing is compared to a starving lion among penned sheep, stressing the helpless victims and his predatory ferocity.
"Supped on vengeance" turns killing into a feast, picking up the wine and gore imagery.
"All for nought" hints that Euryalus will not keep the spoils; the stolen gear leads to his doom.
Night is called a "friend": the darkness is treated as an ally that shelters the fugitives.
Nisus's rapid questions show his desperate indecision before he acts.
Euryalus dying is compared to a cut purple flower and drooping poppies, making his young death beautiful and pitiable.
The poet speaks directly to the dead friends, promising them lasting fame through his own song.
The mother addresses her dead son directly, making her grief immediate and raw.
Helenor charging into the spears is compared to a trapped beast hurling itself at the hunters, conveying desperate courage.
Turnus seizing Lycus is likened to Jove's eagle taking a hare or a wolf taking a lamb, stressing helpless prey.
Numanus's boastful speech paints him as arrogant, and presents Italians as hardy and Trojans as soft.
Ascanius turns Numanus's taunt about "twice-captured Phrygians" back on him, answering words with a fatal arrow.
Battle is likened to a storm of rain and hail, conveying the density and violence of the missiles.
The two giants at the gate are compared to tall oaks beside rivers, stressing their height and steadiness.
The narrator's cry "madman" condemns Pandarus' blunder, and the tiger-among-cattle image shows the disaster.
Flashing eyes, clanging arms and a blood-red crest present Turnus as terrifying and almost supernatural.
The narrator notes that Turnus could have ended the war by admitting his friends, hinting at his fatal flaw.
Turnus is compared to a lion at bay, fierce yet forced to retreat.
